title: Explain how a production REST API handles the five concerns that interviewers probe together — structured error handling (RFC 9457 Problem Details with correct status codes), pagination for large result sets (why cursor/keyset beats offset at depth), API versioning (URL path, header, media-type), idempotency (idempotent HTTP methods plus the Idempotency-Key header for safe retries of POST), and content negotiation (the Accept and Content-Type headers choosing JSON vs XML) — and show how they fit together in real finance code.
shortTitle: REST API — error handling, pagination, versioning, idempotency, content negotiation

s1_definition.profdef: A production REST API treats every business thing as a resource with a stable URL and acts on it using the standard HTTP methods and status codes. Error handling returns a consistent machine-readable body, ideally RFC 9457 Problem Details, with the correct status code rather than a vague 200 plus an error flag. Pagination splits large collections into pages; offset pagination uses LIMIT and OFFSET and degrades at deep pages, while cursor (keyset) pagination remembers the last key seen and seeks forward, staying fast at any depth. API versioning lets the contract evolve without breaking old clients, commonly through a URL path segment such as /api/v1, a custom header, or a media-type. Idempotency means making the same request twice has the same effect as making it once; GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by definition, and POST is made safely retryable with a client-supplied Idempotency-Key. Content negotiation uses the Accept and Content-Type headers so the same endpoint can serve or accept JSON or XML.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India's online system as a very disciplined bank branch. Error handling is the printed rejection slip that always has the same layout, a clear reason, and the right stamp, so Rajesh's mobile app always knows how to read it. Pagination is how the clerk hands you the account statement in neat pages instead of one impossibly long roll — and a smart clerk remembers "last entry you saw was number 500" instead of recounting from the top every time. Versioning is like the bank keeping the old form (v1) valid for existing customers while rolling out a new form (v2) for everyone else. Idempotency is the guarantee that if Rajesh taps "Transfer" twice because his network glitched, the money only moves once. Content negotiation is the clerk asking "do you want this in English or Hindi?" and giving you the format you asked for.
s1_definition.oneliner: A production REST API returns consistent Problem Details errors with correct status codes, paginates with cursors for deep pages, versions its contract, uses Idempotency-Keys so retried POSTs run once, and negotiates JSON or XML through Accept and Content-Type.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A production REST API treats every business thing as a resource with a stable URL and acts on it using the standard HTTP methods and status codes. Error handling returns a consistent machine-readable body, ideally RFC 9457 Problem Details, with the correct status code rather than a vague 200 plus an error flag. Pagination splits large collections into pages; offset pagination uses LIMIT and OFFSET and degrades at deep pages, while cursor (keyset) pagination remembers the last key seen and seeks forward, staying fast at any depth. API versioning lets the contract evolve without breaking old clients, commonly through a URL path segment such as /api/v1, a custom header, or a media-type. Idempotency means making the same request twice has the same effect as making it once; GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by definition, and POST is made safely retryable with a client-supplied Idempotency-Key. Content negotiation uses the Accept and Content-Type headers so the same endpoint can serve or accept JSON or XML.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India's online system as a very disciplined bank branch. Error handling is the printed rejection slip that always has the same layout, a clear reason, and the right stamp, so Rajesh's mobile app always knows how to read it. Pagination is how the clerk hands you the account statement in neat pages instead of one impossibly long roll — and a smart clerk remembers "last entry you saw was number 500" instead of recounting from the top every time. Versioning is like the bank keeping the old form (v1) valid for existing customers while rolling out a new form (v2) for everyone else. Idempotency is the guarantee that if Rajesh taps "Transfer" twice because his network glitched, the money only moves once. Content negotiation is the clerk asking "do you want this in English or Hindi?" and giving you the format you asked for.

**One line to remember:** A production REST API returns consistent Problem Details errors with correct status codes, paginates with cursors for deep pages, versions its contract, uses Idempotency-Keys so retried POSTs run once, and negotiates JSON or XML through Accept and Content-Type.

sections.s2_technical:
Let me walk through each of the five concerns the way an experienced engineer would explain it to a junior joining the payments team, with a small finance code snippet for each so you can see the API actually being used.

Error handling is the first thing that separates a toy API from a production one. The anti-pattern is returning 200 OK with a body like a success flag set to false, because every client then has to parse the body to know whether the call worked, and HTTP caches and monitoring treat a failure as a success. The correct approach is to return the right status code — 404 when a fund does not exist, 400 for bad input, 409 for a conflict — with a consistent RFC 9457 Problem Details body. In Spring you build it directly: `ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Account not found: SAV9999"); pd.setTitle("Account Not Found"); pd.setProperty("accountId", "SAV9999");`. A single `@RestControllerAdvice` class with `@ExceptionHandler` methods turns each domain exception into one of these bodies, so the controller code stays clean and every error looks identical to the client.

Pagination matters the moment a collection grows. Offset pagination is the obvious approach — `SELECT * FROM transactions ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` — but the database still has to walk and discard one hundred thousand rows before returning the next twenty, so page five thousand is painfully slow and new inserts can shift rows between pages. Cursor (keyset) pagination fixes this by remembering the last key seen and querying forward from it: `SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE id > :lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 20`. Because the id column is indexed, the database seeks straight to that point, so the ten-thousandth page is as fast as the first. The API returns a `nextCursor` value that the client sends back to fetch the following page, for example `GET /api/v1/transactions?cursor=TXN-100020&limit=20`.

API versioning lets you change the contract without breaking existing integrations. The most common and most visible approach is a path segment: `GET /api/v1/accounts/SAV2001` today and `GET /api/v2/accounts/SAV2001` when the response shape changes. In Spring you simply map the controllers accordingly: `@RequestMapping("/api/v1/accounts")` on one controller and `@RequestMapping("/api/v2/accounts")` on another. Other styles exist — a custom header such as `X-API-Version: 2` or a versioned media-type like `Accept: application/vnd.bank.v2+json` — but path versioning is the easiest for clients to see and for you to route. The senior point is that v1 must keep working unchanged for as long as customers depend on it.

Idempotency is about making retries safe. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by definition: reading an account twice, replacing it with the same body twice, or deleting it twice leaves the server in the same final state. POST is not idempotent by default — posting a transfer twice would move the money twice. The industry solution is an `Idempotency-Key` header: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it, for example `Idempotency-Key: 7f3b-rajesh-rent-oct`. The server stores the key with the result of the first request; if the same key arrives again, it returns the stored result instead of processing the transfer again. In code this is a check at the top of the handler: `if (idempotencyStore.containsKey(key)) return idempotencyStore.get(key);` before doing the work, then saving the result under that key.

Content negotiation lets one endpoint serve multiple formats. The client states what it wants with the `Accept` header and what it is sending with the `Content-Type` header. If Rajesh's app sends `Accept: application/xml`, Spring serializes the response as XML; if it sends `Accept: application/json`, it returns JSON — the controller code does not change. You enable this by declaring the produced types: `@GetMapping(value = "/{id}", produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, MediaType.APPLICATION_XML_VALUE})`. Spring's `HttpMessageConverter` chain then picks the right converter based on the Accept header. A senior nuance is that if the client asks for a format you cannot produce, you return 406 Not Acceptable rather than silently defaulting.
sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the real situation at National Bank of India before we look at any code, the way I would explain it to a friend who understands banking but not Java.

The bank runs a REST API that powers its mobile app and internet banking site. Customers like Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001, use it to look up accounts, read their transaction history, and move money. The API started simple but is now used by millions of customers, and five separate production problems have forced the team to do things the right way.

Problem 1 — When something goes wrong, the app shows confusing messages. The old API returned 200 OK with a body that sometimes said success was false, so the app could not tell a real failure from a real success, and the monitoring dashboards were useless because every call looked like a success. This is exactly why we return proper status codes with RFC 9457 Problem Details: a missing account returns 404 with a structured body, bad input returns 400, and the app always knows how to display the error.

Problem 2 — Rajesh has fifteen years of transactions, and scrolling to the oldest ones used to take forever. The old API used offset pagination, so fetching page five thousand made the database count and throw away a hundred thousand rows every time. This is exactly why we switch to cursor pagination: the API remembers the last transaction id shown and fetches the next batch starting just after it, so deep pages load instantly.

Problem 3 — The bank wants to change the shape of the account response to add new fields and rename an old one, but it cannot break the thousands of existing app installs still on the old version. This is exactly why we use URL path versioning: the old clients keep calling /api/v1 and get the old shape, while new clients call /api/v2 and get the improved shape.

Problem 4 — Rajesh taps "Pay Rent" on a weak train network, the response is slow, and he taps again. Without protection the bank would transfer his rent twice. This is exactly why we use an Idempotency-Key: the app sends a unique key for that rent payment, and if the same key arrives twice the server returns the first result instead of moving the money again.

Problem 5 — One partner integration consumes XML while the mobile app consumes JSON, and the bank does not want to maintain two separate endpoints. This is exactly why we use content negotiation: the same endpoint serves JSON or XML depending on the Accept header the caller sends.

Now that the problems are clear, here is what each part of the code will do. The Account and Transaction classes are the domain objects. The AccountResponse record is the versioned DTO returned to clients. The AccountNotFoundException and a global handler produce Problem Details error bodies. The PageResponse record carries a page of transactions plus the next cursor. The IdempotencyStore remembers keys and their results. The BankApiService holds the logic: getAccount reads one account, listTransactions does cursor pagination, and transfer applies the idempotency check. The demo wires it all together and prints the output so you can see each concern in action.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the single-file runnable demo
javac BankApiDemo.java

# Run it
java com.bank.api.BankApiDemo

# In a real Spring Boot project you would build and run the jar instead:
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/bank-rest-api-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# Versioning: v1 and v2 live side by side
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001 -H 'Accept: application/json'
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v2/accounts/SAV2001 -H 'Accept: application/json'

# Content negotiation: same endpoint, XML instead of JSON
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v2/accounts/SAV2001 -H 'Accept: application/xml'

# Cursor pagination: follow the nextCursor from the previous page
curl 'http://localhost:8080/api/v2/accounts/SAV2001/transactions?limit=2'
curl 'http://localhost:8080/api/v2/accounts/SAV2001/transactions?cursor=TXN-00002&limit=2'

# Idempotency: retrying with the same key moves money only once
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v2/transfers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Idempotency-Key: 7f3b-rajesh-rent-oct' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CUR3001","amount":50000}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a sequence of real API calls: read Rajesh's account, read a missing account, page through Rajesh's transactions two at a time, and transfer fifty thousand rupees twice with the same idempotency key.

Step 1 — The app calls getAccount for SAV2001. The service reads the account from the repository, finds Rajesh with a balance of ten lakh rupees, and builds a v2 AccountResponse DTO containing only the account id, the holder name, and the balance. The internal version column stays hidden. The output is a clean 200-equivalent object.

Step 2 — The app calls getAccount for SAV9999. The repository returns null, so the service throws an AccountNotFoundException. In a real API this becomes a 404 response with an RFC 9457 Problem Details body carrying a type, a title, a status of 404, a detail message, and the offending account id. The data here is an error object, not a money change.

Step 3 — The app requests the first page of transactions with no cursor and a limit of two. The repository seeks from the start and returns TXN-00001 and TXN-00002. The service sets the next cursor to TXN-00002 and marks hasMore as true. The output is page one plus the cursor the client must send next.

Step 4 — The app requests the next page, sending cursor TXN-00002 and limit two. The repository seeks strictly past TXN-00002 and returns TXN-00003 and TXN-00004. Notice the database never re-reads the first two rows — that is the whole point of cursor pagination. The output is page two plus the new cursor.

Step 5 — The app calls transfer with idempotency key 7f3b-rajesh-rent-oct for fifty thousand rupees from SAV2001 to CUR3001. The key is not in the store, so the service debits Rajesh (his balance becomes nine lakh fifty thousand) and credits Priya (her balance becomes three lakh), creates transfer id TXF-00001, and saves that id under the key. The output is TXF-00001.

Step 6 — The app retries the same transfer with the same key because the network glitched. This time the service finds the key already present and returns the stored TXF-00001 immediately, without touching any balance. Rajesh is debited only once. The output is the same TXF-00001, proving idempotency.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In our banking REST API I treat five concerns as non-negotiable, because together they are what makes an API production-grade rather than a demo. The first is error handling. I never return 200 OK with a success-false flag, because that blinds both clients and monitoring. Instead I return the correct status code — 404 for a missing account, 400 for bad input, 409 for a conflict — with a consistent RFC 9457 Problem Details body built in one @RestControllerAdvice class, so every error the mobile app receives looks identical and is easy to display.

The second is pagination. For Rajesh with fifteen years of transactions, offset pagination is a trap because the database walks and discards every earlier row, so deep pages crawl. I use cursor, or keyset, pagination: the client sends the last transaction id it saw and the query does WHERE id greater than that cursor with an index seek, so page ten thousand is as fast as page one. The response carries a nextCursor the client sends back for the following page.

The third is versioning, which I usually do with a URL path segment so v1 and v2 live side by side and I can evolve the response shape without breaking the thousands of app installs still on the old version. The fourth is idempotency. GET, PUT, and DELETE are naturally idempotent, but POST is not, so for transfers I require an Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the result against that key, and if Rajesh double-taps Pay Rent on a flaky network the retry returns the stored transfer id and the money moves exactly once.

The fifth is content negotiation. One endpoint serves our JSON mobile app and an XML partner integration by honouring the Accept header, and if a client asks for a format we cannot produce we return 406 rather than silently guessing. When I explain this to an interviewer I stress that each of these came from a real production pain — confusing error screens, slow deep pages, a breaking contract change, a double-charged customer, and a partner that needed XML — and that getting all five right is what lets a banking API scale to millions of customers without surprises.

---

keyPoints: GET: read. POST: create. PUT: full replace. PATCH: partial update. DELETE: remove
Idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE — same request, same result
POST is NOT idempotent — may create duplicate
Safe methods: GET, HEAD — do not modify server state
